title: Accruals & prepayments
examples: When do I record an expense if I haven't paid for it yet?
What is the difference between an accrual and a prepayment?
How does the matching principle affect my profit calculation?

explain.say: Today we learn about accruals and prepayments in accounting. These help us follow the matching principle. The matching principle means matching revenues to the expenses that earned them. For example, if you use electricity in December, you must record the electricity cost in December. Screen: Matching Revenue to Expenses

items: Revenue earned in period: Record revenue
Expenses incurred in period: Record expense
Match them: Report in the same period

explain.say: Next we look at prepayments. A prepayment is an expense paid for, but not yet used. For instance, you might pay for a year's insurance premium in advance. You record this as an asset until you actually use it up. Screen: Prepaid Expense Asset

Now let's look at accruals. An accrual is an expense that has been incurred, but not yet paid for. For example, you receive a utility bill in January for December's usage. You must record the expense in December. Screen: Accrued Expense Liability

These adjustments are crucial for accurate reporting. They ensure your profit reflects the correct period's activity. For example, if you paid rent for January and February in advance, you must adjust the books to show only January's expense this month. Screen: Adjusting Entries

items: Date Paid: Paid for two months
End of First Month: Record one month's expense

explain.say: In everyday life, think about your mobile phone plan. You might pay for three months upfront. This is a prepayment. You only expense one month's cost each month as you use the service. Screen: Phone Bill Adjustment

A common mistake is treating all payments as immediate expenses. Students often forget to check if the service period has actually passed. To avoid this, always ask yourself when the benefit was actually received. Screen: Don't Forget Timing

items: Ask: When was the benefit used?

faq.q: What is the main goal of using accruals and prepayments?
faq.a: The main goal is to follow the matching principle. This ensures that the expenses are recorded in the same accounting period as the revenue they helped generate. You might also ask: How do I match costs to sales? Or: Why do I need adjustments?
asks: How do I match costs to sales?

faq.q: If I pay for something in advance, is it an asset or an expense?
faq.a: If you pay for it in advance, it is initially recorded as an asset. It only becomes an expense as you use up the benefit over time. You might also ask: Is prepaid rent an asset? Or: When does prepaid money become an expense?
asks: When does prepaid money become an expense?

faq.q: What is the difference between an accrual and a prepayment?
faq.a: A prepayment is cash paid too early, making it an asset. An accrual is an expense incurred but not yet paid for, making it a liability. You might also ask: Which is a liability? Or: Does accrual mean I owe money?
asks: Does accrual mean I owe money?

faq.q: Do I adjust the books at the end of the year?
faq.a: Yes, adjustments are typically made at the end of an accounting period. This process is necessary to ensure the financial statements are accurate for that specific time frame. You might also ask: When do I make adjustments? Or: Is year-end adjustment mandatory?

faq.q: Can I use the cash basis or the accrual basis?
faq.a: For accurate reporting, the accrual basis is generally required in advanced accounting. This method records transactions when they occur, not just when cash changes hands. You might also ask: What is the accrual basis? Or: Is cash basis okay for business?
asks: Is cash basis okay for business?

facts: The matching principle requires expenses to be recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped generate.
A prepayment is an asset because the company has a right to future service or goods.
An accrual represents a liability because the company owes money for services already received.
Adjusting entries correct accounts to reflect the true economic activity of a period.

quiz.say: A business pays six months' rent in advance on January 1st. At the end of January, what is the correct accounting treatment?

options.show: Debit Rent Expense for one month and credit Accrued Rent.
options.say: Debit Rent Expense for one month and credit Accrued Rent.

options.show: Debit Rent Expense for one month's rent and credit Prepaid Rent for one month's
options.say: Debit Rent Expense for one month's rent and credit Prepaid Rent for one month's

options.show: Debit Rent Expense for six months' rent and credit Cash.
options.say: Debit Rent Expense for six months' rent and credit Cash.

options.show: Debit Prepaid Rent for six months' rent and credit Cash.
options.say: Debit Prepaid Rent for six months' rent and credit Cash.

quiz.why: This correctly applies the prepayment concept, reducing the asset and recording the expense for the period used.

wrong.0: This confuses prepaid expenses with accrued expenses; the payment was made, not the expense received.
wrong.2: This incorrectly records the entire payment as an expense immediately, ignoring the future benefit.
wrong.3: This only records the payment but fails to recognize the expense that has actually occurred in January.

quiz.say: A consultant billed a client for services rendered in December, but the payment will not be received until January. What must the company record in December?

options.show: Debit Cash and credit Service Revenue.
options.say: Debit Cash and credit Service Revenue.

options.show: Debit Service Expense and credit Accounts Payable.
options.say: Debit Service Expense and credit Accounts Payable.

options.show: Do nothing until payment is received in January.
options.say: Do nothing until payment is received in January.

options.show: Debit Accounts Receivable and credit Service Revenue.
options.say: Debit Accounts Receivable and credit Service Revenue.

quiz.why: Since the service was performed in December, the revenue must be recognized in December, creating a receivable asset.

wrong.0: This assumes cash was received in December, which contradicts the information given.
wrong.1: This incorrectly records the service as an expense rather than revenue earned by the company.
wrong.2: This violates the matching principle by delaying revenue recognition until cash is received.

quiz.say: If a company uses up half of its prepaid insurance policy during the month, what entry is required?

options.show: Debit Insurance Expense and credit Prepaid Insurance.
options.say: Debit Insurance Expense and credit Prepaid Insurance.

options.show: Debit Insurance Expense and credit Cash.
options.say: Debit Insurance Expense and credit Cash.

options.show: Debit Prepaid Insurance and credit Insurance Expense.
options.say: Debit Prepaid Insurance and credit Insurance Expense.

options.show: No entry is needed because the payment was already recorded.
options.say: No entry is needed because the payment was already recorded.

quiz.why: The credit reduces the asset (Prepaid Insurance) and the debit records the portion that has now been used up as an expense.

wrong.1: This incorrectly suggests that cash is leaving the business when the insurance was already paid for.
wrong.2: This reverses the entry; the asset must decrease, not the expense account.
wrong.3: This ignores the passage of time and the consumption of the asset, violating the matching principle.
